title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 30
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A council introduced a 20 mph limit on residential streets and reports that recorded collisions on those streets fell by 18 per cent. It concludes that the limit made the streets safer.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Some drivers exceed the new limit.
B. The limit was introduced in stages.
C. Signs were installed at every entry point.
D. Residents welcomed the change.
E. Through traffic diverted onto adjacent main roads, where collisions rose by a similar number.
questions.explanation: Displacement leaves the total unchanged, so a claim about safety cannot rest on the treated streets alone — though it may still be a fair trade if main roads are engineered for the traffic.

questions.prompt: A publisher found that manuscripts submitted through literary agents are accepted at a far higher rate than unsolicited manuscripts, and concludes that agented manuscripts are better written.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Agents charge a percentage of the advance.
B. Agents submit only to publishers whose current list suggests they want that kind of book, while unsolicited manuscripts arrive regardless of fit.
C. Some agented manuscripts are rejected.
D. The publisher receives thousands of submissions a year.
E. Unsolicited manuscripts are read by junior staff.
questions.explanation: Targeting explains the acceptance gap without any difference in quality: the agent's contribution may be matching rather than selecting.

questions.prompt: A gym chain reports that members who book classes in advance attend more often than members who drop in, and plans to require advance booking for all classes.
questions.question: The plan assumes which of the following?
options: A. Classes are currently under-attended.
B. Members own mobile telephones.
C. Instructors prefer known class sizes.
D. The attendance difference reflects the effect of booking rather than the commitment of members who choose to book.
E. Drop-in attendance is falling.
questions.explanation: Booking marks an intention that already exists; requiring it of everyone need not create that intention in members who currently drop in.

questions.prompt: A distillery reports that its whisky matured in barrels previously used for sherry wins more awards than its whisky matured in new oak, and concludes that sherry barrels produce better whisky.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much sherry barrels cost
B. Whether judges know which barrel type they are tasting
C. Whether the sherry-barrel whisky is also matured for longer before bottling
D. How many awards the distillery has won in total
E. Whether the distillery entered more competitions this year
questions.explanation: Maturation time is the obvious confound: if the sherry-barrel spirit sits longer, the comparison measures age as much as wood.

questions.prompt: Every printing press at the Halden works that runs on the night shift is fitted with an automatic ink monitor. No press with an automatic ink monitor has produced a batch rejected for colour variation this quarter. Some presses at the works have produced batches rejected for colour variation.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some presses at the works do not run on the night shift.
B. Ink monitors prevent colour variation.
C. Most presses run on the night shift.
D. Night-shift work produces better quality than day-shift work.
E. Rejected batches come from the oldest presses.
questions.explanation: Presses with rejected batches have no monitor, and night running implies a monitor, so those presses do not run nights. B and D assert causal claims the premises do not support.

questions.prompt: A hospital reports that its new triage system has reduced the average time from arrival to first assessment from 42 minutes to 26. A clinician doubts that patients are being seen sooner.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most supports the clinician's doubt?
options: A. The system was designed by an external consultancy.
B. Staff numbers were unchanged.
C. The department treats 200 patients a day.
D. Waiting areas were refurbished at the same time.
E. First assessment is now recorded when a nurse takes initial details, a step that previously was not counted as an assessment.
questions.explanation: Redefining the endpoint moves the measure without moving the care; the clinically meaningful interval may be unchanged.

questions.prompt: An insurer notes that policyholders who install approved smoke alarms make fewer fire claims, and proposes to offer a discount for installing them.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal's expected saving?
options: A. Approved alarms cost about £30.
B. Alarms must be tested monthly.
C. Households that install approved alarms are those already careful about fire risk, and their claim rate was lower before installing anything.
D. Some households install more alarms than required.
E. Fire claims are the insurer's largest single category.
questions.explanation: If the alarm marks a careful household rather than creating one, a discount rewards behaviour that already existed and buys little reduction in claims.

questions.prompt: A city compared two schemes and reports that its bike-hire scheme costs less per journey than its bus network, and argues that funding should shift from buses to bikes.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. does not account for the cost of docking stations
B. ignores that the two serve different journeys and different people, so cost per journey is not a like-for-like comparison
C. assumes cyclists obey traffic rules
D. relies on a single year of data
E. overlooks seasonal variation in cycling
questions.explanation: A bus carries people who cannot cycle, over distances and in weather that bikes do not serve; equal cost per journey does not make the journeys substitutes.

questions.prompt: A software company reports that customers who contact its support line within the first month are more likely to renew their subscription than customers who do not, and plans to encourage all new customers to make contact.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the plan?
options: A. Support calls cost the company money.
B. Some customers contact support several times.
C. The support line operates during office hours.
D. Customers who contact support are those actively using the product, and it is the use rather than the contact that predicts renewal.
E. Renewal rates are highest among large accounts.
questions.explanation: Prompting contact from customers who are not using the product cannot manufacture the engagement that the correlation actually reflects.

questions.prompt: A supermarket chain argues that its packaging is now more sustainable because the proportion of its packaging that is recyclable rose from 62 per cent to 88 per cent.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: A. Total packaging used rose by half over the same period, so the tonnage that is not recyclable also increased.
B. Recyclable packaging is sometimes more expensive.
C. Some customers do not sort their waste.
D. The chain sells more products than before.
E. Recycling rates vary between local authorities.
questions.explanation: A rising proportion of a growing total can leave more unrecyclable packaging than before, which is what a claim about sustainability has to answer.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to fund a new tram line argue that trams in comparable cities carry more passengers than the bus routes they replaced. Opponents reply that those cities also rebuilt their city centres at the same time.
questions.question: The opponents' reply weakens the supporters' argument by
options: A. denying that trams carry more passengers
B. questioning the cost estimates for the tram line
C. arguing that buses are more flexible
D. showing that the comparable cities are larger
E. identifying a change that could account for the ridership difference independently of the mode
questions.explanation: The reply grants the passenger figures and attacks the attribution, which is the stronger move available on the evidence described.

questions.passageText:
Firms now publish extensive information about their environmental and social conduct, and the volume of it has grown far faster than agreement about what any of it means. The difficulty is not that companies are uniformly dishonest. It is that the reported quantities are of three quite different kinds, and they are presented together as though they were one.

The first kind is measurable and audited in something like the way financial figures are: tonnes of emissions from a firm's own operations, water drawn, waste sent to landfill. These are imperfect but checkable. The second kind is measurable in principle and rests on estimates a firm does not control — emissions embedded in purchased goods, or generated by customers using the product. For many firms this category dwarfs the first, and is calculated from industry averages that a competitor with identical operations might apply differently. The third kind is not a quantity at all: statements about culture, commitment and intent, which cannot be false in the way a number can.

Ratings agencies compress all three into a single score, and the scores of different agencies for the same firm correlate weakly — far less than credit ratings do. That divergence is often reported as evidence of incompetence. It is better read as evidence that the agencies are measuring different things and calling them by the same name.

The reform that would help most is unglamorous: separating the categories in disclosure so that a reader can see which figures are audited, which are estimated, and which are assertions. Aggregation is what destroys the information, and it is performed downstream of the firms that are usually blamed for the result.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the second kind of reported quantity differs from the first in that it
options: A. is audited more rigorously
B. concerns culture and intent rather than measurement
C. is required by fewer jurisdictions
D. rests on estimates the firm does not control and is often far larger
E. is reported only by large firms
questions.explanation: Emissions embedded in purchased goods or arising from customer use are calculated from industry averages another firm might apply differently.

questions.passageText:
Living things absorb carbon from the atmosphere, including a small proportion of the unstable isotope carbon-14. Absorption stops at death and the isotope decays at a known rate, so the proportion remaining in a sample indicates how long ago the organism died. The principle is simple, and almost everything interesting about the method lies in the corrections.

The first is that atmospheric carbon-14 has not been constant. Production varies with solar activity and the Earth's magnetic field, so a raw radiocarbon age is not a calendar age. Calibration curves built from tree rings of known age, and extended by corals and lake sediments, convert one to the other — which is why radiocarbon dates are quoted with a calibrated range rather than a single year, and why the range is sometimes wide and oddly shaped where the curve flattens.

Two industrial effects complicate the recent past. Burning fossil fuels released carbon containing no carbon-14, diluting the atmospheric proportion; atmospheric nuclear testing then roughly doubled it. The result is that samples from the last two centuries can be dated with unusual precision, because the sharp spike gives a distinctive signature, while the century before that is unusually difficult.

The method's limits are as important as its reach. It dates the death of an organism, not the event an archaeologist cares about: charcoal in a hearth may come from wood already old when burned. It is useless beyond about fifty thousand years, when too little carbon-14 remains. And it says nothing at all about materials that were never alive, which is why a stone tool can only be dated through what is found alongside it.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a raw radiocarbon age must be calibrated because
options: A. atmospheric carbon-14 has not been constant over time
B. decay rates vary with temperature
C. samples absorb carbon after death
D. tree rings decay at a different rate
E. laboratories use different equipment
questions.explanation: Production varies with solar activity and the magnetic field, so calibration curves convert radiocarbon years to calendar years.

questions.passageText:
Most cities require a building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, set by formulas that vary between jurisdictions and are rarely derived from anything measured. The requirements are usually presented as a technical matter. Their effects are not.

A required space is not free. It occupies land, costs money to build — more where it must go underground — and that cost is folded into the rent or price of whatever the building contains. The parking is then supplied to the driver at no charge, which is not the absence of a cost but a decision about who pays it: the tenant of the flat who owns no car, the customer of the shop who arrived on foot, the employee who takes a bus.

The consequences compound. Minimums force buildings apart, which lengthens the distances between them and makes walking less useful, which raises the demand for driving that the minimums were set to accommodate. They also make small sites unbuildable, since a modest building cannot absorb the land its required parking consumes, which removes precisely the incremental development that fills gaps in an existing street.

The reform is not to ban parking but to stop requiring it, letting developers supply what buyers will pay for, and to price kerbside parking so that the public space is not given away at a price of zero while private space is mandated. Cities that have removed minimums have not seen parking disappear; they have seen less of it built, and built where someone judged it worth the cost.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, parking minimums are usually presented as
options: A. a subsidy to drivers
B. a response to measured demand
C. a source of municipal revenue
D. a technical matter
E. a constraint on small developers
questions.explanation: The passage's argument is that their effects are not technical, and that the formulas are rarely derived from anything measured.

options: A. Minimums push buildings apart, which makes walking less useful, which raises the driving the minimums accommodate
B. Higher parking charges reduce driving, which reduces revenue
C. More parking attracts more residents, who require more parking
D. Underground parking raises rents, which attracts wealthier tenants
E. Small sites become unbuildable, which raises land values

questions.passageText:
A recipe seems a straightforward document: a list of ingredients and a sequence of operations. Historically it is nothing of the kind, and the change in what recipes contain records a change in who was expected to read them.

Early written recipes assume a cook who already knows how to cook. They name ingredients without quantities, give times by reference to other processes — cook until it is done, bake while a loaf bakes — and omit steps that anyone in a kitchen would perform without being told. They are aids to memory for a practitioner, not instructions for a novice.

Standardised quantities arrived with standardised measures, and both arrived with a readership that could not be assumed to have learned in a kitchen. The nineteenth-century cookery book addressed a household without a trained cook, and its precision is a response to that reader rather than an advance in technique. The same shift explains the appearance of the oven temperature, which required ovens whose temperature could be known.

What has not changed is that a recipe underdetermines the dish. It cannot specify the size of the pan, the strength of the heat, the moisture of the flour, or what the result should look like at each stage, and the experienced cook supplies all of it without noticing. This is why written recipes travel badly between cuisines whose unstated assumptions differ, and why a cook working from an unfamiliar tradition may follow every instruction exactly and produce something the author would not recognise.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, early written recipes omitted steps because they
options: A. were copied from oral sources
B. were written for professional guilds only
C. were constrained by the cost of paper
D. had to be memorised
E. assumed a reader who already knew how to cook
questions.explanation: They are described as aids to memory for a practitioner rather than instructions for a novice.

The consequences compound. Minimums force buildings apart, which lengthens the distances between them and makes walking less useful, which raises the demand for driving that the minimums were set to accommodate. They also make small sites unbuildable, since a modest building cannot absorb the land its required parking consumes, which removes precisely the incremental development that fills gaps in an existing street.

The reform is not to ban parking but to stop requiring it, letting developers supply what buyers will pay for, and to price kerbside parking so that the public space is not given away at a price of zero while private space is mandated. Cities that have removed minimums have not seen parking disappear; they have seen less of it built, and built where someone judged it worth the cost.

readingPassages.title: Writing Down a Recipe
readingPassages.text:
A recipe seems a straightforward document: a list of ingredients and a sequence of operations. Historically it is nothing of the kind, and the change in what recipes contain records a change in who was expected to read them.

Early written recipes assume a cook who already knows how to cook. They name ingredients without quantities, give times by reference to other processes — cook until it is done, bake while a loaf bakes — and omit steps that anyone in a kitchen would perform without being told. They are aids to memory for a practitioner, not instructions for a novice.

Standardised quantities arrived with standardised measures, and both arrived with a readership that could not be assumed to have learned in a kitchen. The nineteenth-century cookery book addressed a household without a trained cook, and its precision is a response to that reader rather than an advance in technique. The same shift explains the appearance of the oven temperature, which required ovens whose temperature could be known.

What has not changed is that a recipe underdetermines the dish. It cannot specify the size of the pan, the strength of the heat, the moisture of the flour, or what the result should look like at each stage, and the experienced cook supplies all of it without noticing. This is why written recipes travel badly between cuisines whose unstated assumptions differ, and why a cook working from an unfamiliar tradition may follow every instruction exactly and produce something the author would not recognise.
